findings.text: The first paragraph tells a newcomer plainly what Athena is and what makes it different. The next two paragraphs explain what a study is and why this page exists, so the reader is oriented right away.
findings.source: "Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository. It shows how it read the request, has one AI model do the work and a different one check it, and records what each step cost."

findings.text: The URL is Athena's site, but almost the whole page is about another project, firstmate. Athena gets only three sentences. A newcomer learns what Athena can do from this one example, but not what using it is like or what it costs to run.
findings.source: <title>Athena explains how firstmate handles work</title> / header ledes

findings.text: There is a clear next step: a link at the top jumps to concrete actions (the repo link, ./setup.sh, athena ask "add a changelog"). But the page does not give prerequisites, say what kind of checkout setup.sh expects, or say whether API keys or particular AI models are needed. A newcomer has to go to the repo before they can try it.
findings.source: "Next step: install Athena or read firstmate itself" and the Next steps section

findings.text: Firstmate is explained clearly, and the problem it solves (workers overwriting each other's files, starting each agent by hand) is stated. The "Words used first" list defines terms before they are used, which helps.
findings.source: Heading "What firstmate is": "keeps a backlog of programming tasks and hands each one to a worker ... so that several tasks can run side by side"

findings.text: "Captain call" is used again and again but is never defined, neither in "Words used first" nor in the Glossary. The same goes for "endpoint", "brief", "durable record" and "harness pin". A newcomer cannot follow the reopen path or the relaunch details.
findings.source: "If the backlog item is still an open captain call, teardown reopens it instead of closing it."

findings.text: From the States section onward, the page reads like a specification: state machines, exit codes, self-transitions. That serves a reviewer, not a newcomer. The page does not say these sections are optional for a first read.
findings.source: Transitions cards t2 "queued → queued", t10 "ready → ready"; "exits 75 ... exits 1"

findings.text: Each claim is traced to file lines at a pinned commit, and the page says openly that nothing was run. A newcomer can check this. It also shows Athena's main selling point.
findings.source: "Each statement below ends with the id of the claim that supports it" and Limits f1: "no failure or retry edge was observed; every claim is marked read"

findings.text: The page is honest about gaps (in scope, no captain deadline, no relaunch bound), which builds trust. But defining a term as undefined may leave a newcomer unsure what yolo actually allows.
findings.source: "in scope ... The cited instruction does not say what makes work in scope, so this page gives no test for it."

findings.text: This closing note, and the footer, refer to Athena's internal folder layout. To a first-time visitor they mean nothing.
findings.source: Heading "About this page": "the name of the folder under studies/ that holds the data this page is generated from"
